Hazard_Description:
During the initial phase of the E-2301 cooler scope, a first-pass inspection was conducted on the sealing faces of the cooler shell, distributor, and head/front cover. At that time, no concerns or damage were identified.

When I subsequently returned with Glacier to carry out the detailed inspection, it was identified that an adjacent work party had stored tools directly on the cooler front cover & sealing face. Following removal of the tools, a small area of mechanical damage was evident on the sealing face.
Action_Taken:
A temporary cover was cable-tied over the cooler front cover in an attempt to prevent any further damage to the sealing surface.

This is not the first concern raised regarding damage to sealing faces/flanges, and the issue needs to be addressed. E-2301 is a critical shutdown scope, and we do not have the machining capability available onboard to restore a sealing face should damage extend across a significant portion of the surface or exceed acceptable limits.

Any further damage could therefore have a direct impact on the integrity of the equipment and the shutdown schedule. If the cooler were subsequently found to leak due to damage to a sealing surface, removing the equipment again would be extremely time-consuming and would require the coordination of multiple teams, creating a significant additional workload and potential schedule impact.

Furthermore, depending on the specific cooler design and service, the affected sealing face may form part of the hydrocarbon pressure boundary. Any damage to such a surface therefore has the potential to become a process safety and containment concern, in addition to the mechanical and schedule implications.

Given the criticality of this equipment and the repeated concerns regarding damage to sealing faces/flanges, all personnel working in the area need to ensure that no tools, equipment, materials, or other items are placed on or against machined sealing surfaces.

This is a very basic site rule that is not being adhered to -  this leads to a drop in standards throughout and sets a bad example of how we look after the asset.
There's also the potential for contamination between the oily coveralls and food as the salad bar and fruit counter are adjacent to this queue.
Action_Taken:
Spoken to guys when I've seen them in there with coveralls and made them aware of the site standards.
I'll make large yellow signs to put on the galley access doors to remind the crew - No Boots or Coveralls in the galley area.

Hazard_Description: Operations reported an issue with starting the lube oil top-up pump P-1170. Following an investigation, it was identified that the low-level switch LSLL-021 on the fresh oil tank was the source of the fault. A full loop check was carried out to determine the location of the fault within the loop. It was found that junction box JB X-1100-01 had corroded away from its mounting plates and was lying on the floor in a very poor condition. The gland plate had also disintegrated, leaving exposed 110V terminals open to the atmosphere within a zoned area. The terminals inside the junction box were heavily corroded, which was determined to be the cause of the fault. See attached photographs
Action_Taken: The issue was immediately reported to the E&I MTL. I then raised an ICC to isolate all loops passing through the junction box, removing the potential for a spark within the zoned area. A replacement junction box was sourced from stores for perpetration works, and planning is now underway to replace the junction box as soon as possible.

Hazard_Description:
When carrying out final gap voltage checks on the LP5 vibration probes, we decided it was good practice to carry out the same checks on HP5, as the vibration routine was not currently being completed on this machine.

During these checks, three probe gap voltages were found to have changed significantly since they were last recorded. Further investigation identified that all three probes were loose at the NPT fitting into the gearbox, which explained the change in gap voltage. In addition, a mist of oil was observed atomising from around the NPT threads of probe 11/5-YE-151-5A where it entered the casing.
Action_Taken:
The issue was reported to the E&I MTL and AA upon discovery. A lube oil isolation was created and applied, and a WCC was raised to allow the issues to be rectified safely. All affected probes and housings were removed, inspected, resealed and securely refitted to the machine. The gap voltages were then set up.

Identifying these issues while the HP5 was already isolated with the hood removed allowed the repairs to be completed efficiently and prevented the need for an additional machine shut down and large work scope at a later date. It also reduced the risk of a potential spurious gearbox vibration trip caused by incorrect probe readings.

A full new set of gap voltages for all probes were taken and recorded. No further issues.
